1.title: Understand electric vehicle markets
1.intro: Electric vehicles are sold as cars, vans, buses and special vehicles.
pts: Segments: personal, delivery vans, buses, trucks, small special vehicles.
Customers: fleets, cities, households. Fleets care about total cost of ownership.
Incentives and rules change; check federal and provincial programmes.
Pick one niche, such as delivery vans in cold climates.
Ride in or drive one electric vehicle for a week and note range loss in cold weather.
Interview five fleet managers: daily distance, depot parking, power at the depot and what they pay now per kilometre.
Total cost of ownership = purchase price + running costs over the years - resale value. Write it for one vehicle you would replace.
1.ex: A delivery fleet compares 10-year cost: if an electric van costs 15,000 more to buy but saves 3,000 a year in fuel and servicing, the saving over 10 years is 30,000, so the van is ahead by 15,000 and pays back in 15,000 / 3,000 = 5 years. Teaching figures in CAD; use the fleet's real numbers.
1.act: Write a niche statement and customer profile.

2.title: Know vehicle rules
2.intro: Vehicles must meet safety and environmental standards.
pts: Federal motor-vehicle safety standards apply before a vehicle can be sold.
Battery transport and storage have dangerous-goods rules.
Provinces register and insure vehicles.
Warranty and recall rules protect buyers.
Check charging time on a home plug, a public charger and a fast charger, and compare with spec.
A vehicle built in small numbers may have different import or approval steps; check the federal and provincial rule for your case.
Keep a certificate file with the standard, the test result, the date and the person who signed.
2.ex: Row: 'Sell a new vehicle | federal safety standards | certify and label | before first sale | certificate on file'. For a 60 kWh battery on a 7 kW home charger, a full charge takes about 60 / 7 = 8.6 hours, which you compare with the stated spec.
2.act: Build a rules table for a small manufacturer.
2.std: Each row has source and date.

3.title: Design the vehicle systems
pts: Define use: range, payload, charging time, cold performance.
Size battery from energy per kilometre.
Plan safety: crash structure, thermal management, battery protection.
Document specifications in one table.
List the five parts that fail most often in fleet use and plan spares.
Add a margin for ageing and cold weather to the pack size, and state the margin you used.
Check payload: weight of the battery, body, driver and cargo against the vehicle's rated limit.
3.ex: Need 250 km at 0.35 kWh per km: 250 x 0.35 = 87.5 kWh usable. Add 20% for cold and ageing: 87.5 x 1.2 = 105 kWh pack. If the cells give 0.15 kWh per kg, the cells alone weigh 105 / 0.15 = 700 kg, which must fit the payload plan.
3.act: Calculate pack size for a chosen use.

4.title: Cost the product
4.intro: Cost per vehicle drives the business.
pts: Bill of materials: battery, motor, body, electronics.
Assembly labour and facility cost per vehicle.
Warranty provision.
Margin and break-even.
Study one crash test report and note what the structure does.
Ask three suppliers for a quote at 100, 500 and 1,000 units and note how the price falls with volume.
Test a 10% rise in battery cost and show the new margin.
4.ex: Price 48,000; cost 36,000; margin 12,000 (25%); fixed cost 3.1M per year gives 3,100,000 / 12,000 = 258.3, so break-even is 259 vehicles, shown as about 260. If battery cost is 14,000 of the 36,000, a 10% rise adds 1,400, so cost is 37,400, margin 10,600 and break-even rises to about 293. Teaching figures in CAD.
4.act: Build a bill of materials and break-even.

5.title: Build to quality
pts: Incoming inspection of parts.
End-of-line tests: brakes, battery, software, leaks.
Traceability by vehicle number.
Corrective action when tests fail.
Interview a fleet mechanic about what is hard to repair.
Set a pass limit for each test and a sign-off line, so no vehicle leaves without a signed sheet.
Count first-pass rate (vehicles that pass the first time divided by vehicles tested) and chart it weekly.
5.ex: End-of-line fail rate 4% mostly connectors; fix with a torque check. At 260 vehicles a year, 4% is about 10 vehicles needing rework; if the torque check halves the fails to 2%, rework drops to about 5.

6.title: Sell and service
pts: Sales through fleets and dealers.
Service network and parts.
Training for technicians.
Remote monitoring.
Write down the software update promise and who delivers it.
Plan service in cold regions: where a customer can get help in winter and how long the repair takes.
Agree a response time for a stopped vehicle and measure it.
6.ex: Fleet pilot: 3 vans for 90 days; uptime 97%. The 3 vans have 3 x 90 = 270 van-days, and 3% down is about 8 van-days lost, which you compare with the offer's target.

7.title: Manage safety and supply risk
7.intro: Batteries and supply chains carry risk.
pts: Battery fire plan and training.
Supplier diversification.
Material sourcing and recycling.
Cyber security for connected vehicles.
Compare the weight of your design with two similar vehicles.
Ask each supplier where its materials come from and how they are recycled; note anything you cannot verify.
Write who you call, and what staff do, in the first ten minutes of a battery incident, and practise it.
7.ex: Risk: 'Cell supplier delay | 4 x 4 = 16 | second source | purchasing | monthly'. A score of 16 out of 25 is high, so the second supplier should be qualified before volume production.

8.title: Pilot and plan scale
pts: Build 5 pilot vehicles.
Measure range, faults and customer feedback.
Stop rule: range under 85% of spec means redesign.
Plan funding and plant.
Record every test in one table: date, condition, result, action.
Measure range in cold weather, in warm weather and loaded, not only on a good day.
Check programme rules and dates for funding yourself, and compare leasing a plant with building one.
8.ex: Range 92% of spec: if the spec is 250 km, 0.92 x 250 = 230 km, above the stop line of 0.85 x 250 = 212.5 km, so proceed. A cold-weather test that gave 200 km would be 80% and trigger a redesign.

quiz: Energy per kilometre times range with a margin.
Why add a margin to battery size?
Cold weather and ageing reduce capacity.
What is total cost of ownership?
Purchase plus running costs over time.
To avoid a single point of failure.
What triggers redesign in the pilot?
